meta.title: Who really said "Age before beauty. Pearls before swine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dorothy Parker probably coined the riposte, but Clare Boothe Luce denied the doorway story and the only eyewitness named a chorus girl instead.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Age before beauty. Pearls before swine'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator credits Parker with the retort but calls the circumstances ambiguous. Luce denied it, and no work by Parker contains the line.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and Algonquin Round Table wit
answer.sourceLine: Only the second half is Parker’s — “age before beauty” was already a stock pleasantry in American print by 1850. Parker never wrote the retort down; it survives purely in other people’s tellings from the mid-to-late 1930s onward, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes she originated the gibe but that the circumstances are ambiguous.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Dorothy Parker, in conversation — no text by her contains it
Walter Winchell, “On Broadway,” June 1936 (woman unnamed); The Spectator (London), 16 September 1938
Clare Boothe Luce, from 14 October 1938 — who denied it in 1970
Quote Investigator, “Dialogue Origin: ‘Age Before Beauty’ ‘Pearls Before Swine’”

source.excerpt: “Age before beauty, Mrs. Parker.” — “And pearls before swine,” said Mrs. Parker, sweeping in.
trail: “Age before beauty” long predates Parker. Word Histories ↗ gives as its earliest instance the New-Orleans Weekly Delta of 3 June 1850: “Age before beauty,” as the chambermaid said as she made room for the old lady. Quote Investigator separately records an 1896 schoolboy version answered with “Men before monkeys.”

The Parker anecdote surfaces in the mid-1930s without a named antagonist. Word Histories notes that Walter Winchell told it in his On Broadway column in June 1936, calling the other woman only “a rival wit”; Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes an anonymous Spectator telling of 16 September 1938 in which she is “a snooty debutante.”

Clare Boothe’s name arrives on 14 October 1938, in Sheilah Graham’s syndicated Hollywood column — Quote Investigator cites the Hartford Courant, Word Histories ↗ the Salt Lake Telegram, both that day. Graham opened it with “Dorothy Parker tells me…”, so the naming traces back to Parker rather than to a witness.

The doubts are nearly as old as the story. The New Yorker called it “the familiar but apocryphal incident” in January 1941; Luce denied it flatly in 1970; and the one eyewitness Quote Investigator ↗ could find, Mrs. Robert Benchley, said it happened at the Algonquin with “some little chorus girl.”
source.excerptNote: As transcribed from The Spectator (London), 16 September 1938, by Quote Investigator ↗. The paragraph is anonymous and second-hand: it introduces the scene with “It is recorded that…” and identifies the other woman only as a debutante.

source.rightsNote: No work by Dorothy Parker is known to contain this line — it exists only inside other people’s reports, and the oldest of those are 1930s newspaper and magazine paragraphs, all published after 1930 and none of them automatically in the public domain. With no identifiable work to anchor a first-publication date to, quotle.info asserts no copyright status for the wording.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: About Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and Algonquin Round Table wit
author.bio: Dorothy Parker was the fastest voice at the Algonquin Round Table, the daily New York lunch table that turned the wisecrack into a spectator sport. She reviewed theatre for Vanity Fair and then The New Yorker, published the verse collections Enough Rope (1926), Sunset Gun (1928) and Death and Taxes (1931), and won the O. Henry Award in 1929 for her story “Big Blonde.” Her reputation for the instant retort is exactly why lines like this one stick to her — and exactly why each one has to be checked.

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong with the popular version
misattribution.intro: The line is a two-hander, and almost every element of the staging is unstable — the other speaker, the setting, even whether the exchange happened. The only stable part is Parker’s four words.

items.why: Luce’s name attaches only on 14 October 1938, in Sheilah Graham’s syndicated Hollywood column. Asked about it by biographer John Keats in 1970, Luce answered: “The ‘Age before beauty’ story is completely apocryphal. Certainly no such remark by me or rejoinder by her was made.” Quote Investigator ↗

items.who: An unnamed debutante — or a chorus girl
items.why: The Spectator version of 16 September 1938 names only “a snooty debutante,” and the sole eyewitness Quote Investigator locates — Mrs. Robert Benchley, recalling it at eighty — put the exchange in the Algonquin dining room with “some little chorus girl.” Quote Investigator ↗

By a 2003 retelling in the Waterloo, Iowa Courier, Luce had been swapped out for Lady Astor and the doorway relocated to a New York hotel — a clean example of an anecdote recasting itself. Word Histories ↗

“Age before beauty” was already a printed joke — Word Histories ↗ finds it in the New-Orleans Weekly Delta of 3 June 1850: “as the chambermaid said as she made room for the old lady.” “Pearls before swine” is Matthew 7:6 King James Bible ↗. Parker’s contribution is the collision and the timing, not the vocabulary.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict, which this page adopts: “QI believes that the originator of the joke is Parker, but the circumstances are ambiguous.” Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why the story keeps changing
lead: An anecdote is a living thing, and this one has been improved in transit. The oldest tellings have no antagonist worth naming — Walter Winchell’s June 1936 column called her only “a rival wit,” and the anonymous paragraph in The Spectator of 16 September 1938 made her “a snooty debutante.” Within a month, Sheilah Graham’s Hollywood column had cast Clare Boothe in the part, and the story finally had the shape it needed: two famous, mutually unimpressed women in a doorway.

That is the mechanism worth noticing. A joke survives on its own merits; the staging around it gets rewritten to whatever makes the better story. Parker’s half of the exchange has stayed word-for-word identical since 1936. Everything else — who spoke first, where they were standing, whether it happened at all — has been swapped out repeatedly.
detailsBody: The New Yorker was sceptical almost immediately. Its January 1941 profile of Clare Boothe referred to “the familiar but apocryphal incident” of the two women entering a restaurant together, retelling the exchange only to flag it as a tale. That is a contemporary publication, three years after the story broke, declining to vouch for it.

Bennett Cerf’s 1944 bestseller Try and Stop Me moved it to a society dinner and left the other woman unnamed but unmistakable — “a beautiful and catty lady-playwright.” By a 2003 newspaper retelling the antagonist had become Lady Astor, at a New York hotel door. The joke never changes; the cast list always does.
context.pull: The joke is Parker’s. The doorway is anyone’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes that Parker originated the joke but that the circumstances are ambiguous; it transcribes The Spectator of 16 September 1938 (other woman = "a snooty debutante"), Sheilah Graham's Hartford Courant column of 14 October 1938 naming Clare Boothe, a January 1941 New Yorker profile calling the incident "apocryphal", Clare Boothe Luce's 1970 denial to John Keats ("completely apocryphal"), Bennett Cerf's 1944 Try and Stop Me version with "a beautiful and catty lady-playwright", an 1896 "Age before beauty" / "Men before monkeys" antecedent, and Mrs. Robert Benchley's eyewitness account placing it at the Algonquin with "some little chorus girl".

Wikiquote lists "Age Before Beauty." "Pearls Before Swine." under its Attributed section for Dorothy Parker, with a note that it is commonly attributed to Parker and Clare Boothe Luce, footnoted to Quote Investigator. Confirmed against the page's raw wikitext, where the entry sits under == Attributed ==.

Word Histories gives the earliest instance of "age before beauty" as the New-Orleans Weekly Delta of Monday 3 June 1850 ("'Age before beauty,' as the chambermaid said as she made room for the old lady"); transcribes Sheilah Graham's Salt Lake Telegram column of Friday 14 October 1938 verbatim, beginning "Dorothy Parker tells me of the last time she encountered Playwright Clare Boothe"; notes Walter Winchell mentioned the anecdote in his On Broadway column in June 1936 without naming the woman, calling her only "a rival wit"; and cites a Waterloo, Iowa Courier retelling of 11 May 2003 that substitutes Lady Astor at a New York hotel.

Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker's dates as born 22 August 1893 (Long Branch, New Jersey) and died 7 June 1967 (New York City), describes her as "an American poet, literary critic and writer of fiction" and a screenwriter, a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, a Vanity Fair theatre critic and New Yorker drama reviewer, and lists Enough Rope (1926), Sunset Gun (1928), Death and Taxes (1931) and the 1929 O. Henry Award for "Big Blonde". The article does not mention the "age before beauty" exchange.

Wikipedia gives Clare Boothe Luce's dates as 10 March 1903 – 9 October 1987 and describes her as a writer and playwright (The Women, 1936), U.S. Representative from Connecticut (1943–1947) and U.S. Ambassador to Italy (1953–1956). The article does not mention the "age before beauty" / "pearls before swine" exchange.

The King James Version text of Matthew 7:6 reads: "Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you."
